concepts.name: Authorship, Discovery, and Dating of the Arthashastra
key_dimensions: R. Shamasastry's discovery and publication (1909) from Mysore Oriental Library manuscripts
Debate over single authorship vs. later interpolations — Kautilya, Vishnugupta, Chanakya as same or different persons
Internal textual evidence vs. external corroboration (Megasthenes' Indica, Ashoka's edicts) for dating
UPSC trap: Arthashastra was 'lost' for centuries — contrast with Indica which was never a single surviving text

concepts.name: Structure and Classification of the Arthashastra as a Text
key_dimensions: 15 Books (Adhikaranas), 150 chapters, 180 topics, ~6,000 shlokas — significance of this encyclopaedic scope
Relationship to earlier Nitishastra and Dandaniti traditions — Kautilya's synthesis vs. predecessors like Brihaspati and Ushanas
Arthashastra as a 'shastric' text: normative prescription vs. descriptive reality trap for UPSC
Comparison with Manusmriti (dharmic law) vs. Arthashastra (statecraft/political economy) — overlapping yet distinct domains

concepts.name: Saptanga Theory — The Seven Elements of the State
key_dimensions: Seven constituents: Swami (king), Amatya (ministers), Janapada (territory/population), Durga (fortified capital), Kosha (treasury), Danda (army), Mitra (ally)
Hierarchical importance debate — Kautilya's own ranking and why Swami heads but Kosha is disproportionately emphasized
UPSC trap: Saptanga vs. modern state elements — territory, population, government, sovereignty mapping exercise
Comparison with Arthashastra's Saptanga and Kautilya's view that a weak king with strong other elements can still govern

concepts.name: Kautilya's Concept of Rajadharma and the Ideal King
key_dimensions: King's happiness subordinated to subjects' happiness — 'Praja sukhe sukham rajnah' — welfare-state implication
Qualities of an ideal king: intellect (Anvikshaki), triple Vedas knowledge, Varta (economics), Dandaniti (political science)
Daily routine (Ashtakaala schedule) of the king — administrative discipline as governance principle
Distinction from Dharmashastra ideal king — Arthashastra king is pragmatic-realist, not just dharmic

concepts.name: Mantriparishad (Council of Ministers) — Composition and Functions
key_dimensions: Distinction between Mantriparishad (council) and individual Amatyas (ministers/officials) — UPSC frequently conflates these
Qualifications for ministers: hereditary background, intellectual ability, moral integrity — meritocratic vs. hereditary tension
Secret testing (upadhana/tester spies) of ministers' loyalty across four temptations: dharma, artha, kama, bhaya
Comparison with Megasthenes' account of royal council — corroboration and contradictions

concepts.name: Espionage System (Gudhapurusha) and Secret Service
key_dimensions: Categories of spies: Sanstha (stationary) vs. Sanchari (wandering/mobile) — five types of Sanstha spies (Kapatikas, Udasthas, etc.)
Use of spies in internal administration: testing officials, monitoring dissent, gathering market intelligence
Women spies (Vishakanya, female ascetics) — unique Kautilyan innovation often asked in Prelims
UPSC trap: Distinguish Arthashastra's systematic spy network from casual intelligence gathering described in other texts

concepts.name: Revenue Administration and the Kosha (Treasury)
key_dimensions: Sources of revenue: land tax (bhaga — 1/6th to 1/4th), customs duties, fines, forest produce, mines, and state enterprises
Concept of 'Sitadhyaksha' (Superintendent of Crown Lands) — state's direct agricultural role
Kautilya's warning against excessive taxation — 'a king who imposes heavy taxes is like a man cutting the udder of a cow'
UPSC trap: Bhaga (share of produce) vs. Bali (voluntary tribute/religious offering) vs. Kara (tax) — three distinct revenue terms

concepts.name: Land Revenue System and Agricultural Policy
key_dimensions: State's role in irrigation — construction of tanks, canals; Setubandha concept and state obligation
Settlement of waste lands (janapada-nivesa) — state-sponsored colonisation and its revenue implications
Graduated taxation based on land quality: irrigated vs. rain-fed vs. forest land
Forced labour (vishti) in agriculture and public works — distinction from slavery (dasa) in Arthashastra

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Labour Laws and Regulation of Workers/Guilds
key_dimensions: Sreni (guilds) as semi-autonomous economic units — state regulation without state ownership
Protection of workers' wages, working conditions — superintendent of weaving (Sutradhyaksha) regulations
State's role in fixing prices through Panyadhyaksha (Superintendent of Trade) — controlled economy elements
UPSC trap: Arthashastra's guild regulation vs. later medieval guild autonomy — earlier state had MORE control

concepts.name: Mandala Theory of Foreign Policy (Rajamandala)
key_dimensions: Concentric circle theory: immediate neighbour is natural enemy, neighbour's neighbour is natural friend
12-element Mandala: Vijigishu (conqueror), Ari (enemy), Madhyama (middle king), Udasina (neutral) and their compounds
Six-fold policy (Shadgunya): Sandhi, Vigraha, Asana, Yana, Samshraya, Dvaidhibhava — each with specific conditions for use
UPSC trap: Sandhi (peace) is NOT permanent friendship — it is a tactical pause; Arthashastra's realism vs. idealism

concepts.name: Four Upayas (State Strategies) for Dealing with Enemies/Subjects
key_dimensions: Sama (conciliation), Dana (gifts/bribery), Bheda (division/sowing dissent), Danda (force) — sequential preference order
Kautilya's prioritisation: Danda as LAST resort for external enemies but used more readily internally — UPSC trap
Application to internal rebellions, frontier tribes, and enemy states — context-dependent use
Comparison with later texts: Manusmriti's similar four upayas — Arthashastra more systematic and tactical

concepts.name: Judicial System and Dharmasthiya Courts
key_dimensions: Two types of courts: Dharmasthiya (civil matters — property, marriage, contracts) vs. Kantakasodhana (criminal/thorns of society)
Three-judge panels (Dharmastha) with defined jurisdiction and appeal mechanisms
Elaborate law of evidence: witnesses, documents, ordeals — Kautilya's skepticism of ordeals vs. Dharmashastra acceptance
UPSC trap: Arthashastra's legal system is more secular and procedural than Manusmriti's religiously-embedded jurisprudence

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Treatment of Slavery (Dasa System)
key_dimensions: Seven categories of slaves in Arthashastra — hereditary, purchased, gifted, self-sold, captured in war, etc.
Legal protections for slaves: right to earn, restrictions on masters' cruelty — relatively more humane than contemporary Greek slavery
Aryan (upper varna) cannot be enslaved — caste-slavery intersection and UPSC trap
Comparison with Megasthenes' claim that 'Indians have no slaves' — the contradiction and scholarly resolution

concepts.name: Position of Women in the Arthashastra
key_dimensions: Women's property rights: stridhana concept, inheritance, widow remarriage provisions
Regulated prostitution (Ganika system) — Ganikadhyaksha (Superintendent of Prostitutes) as state revenue source
Women in espionage and military roles — female bodyguards of the king mentioned
UPSC trap: Arthashastra gives women MORE legal protections than Manusmriti in certain areas (e.g., divorce, remarriage rights)

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Economic Philosophy: State vs. Market
key_dimensions: State monopolies in strategic sectors: mines, forests, armaments, salt — rationale and administration
Regulated private trade with state price supervision — neither pure free market nor command economy
Concept of 'Vishti' (forced/corvée labour) for public works alongside hired labour
Proto-Keynesian elements: state spending on public works during famines — Kautilya as ancient welfare economist argument

concepts.name: Military Organisation and the Concept of Chaturanga Bala
key_dimensions: Four-fold army: Hasty (elephants), Ashva (cavalry), Ratha (chariots), Pada (infantry) — relative importance and deployment
Hereditary army (maula) vs. hired troops (bhrita) vs. guild armies (shreni) vs. allied forces (mitra) — UPSC trap on classifications
Senapati's role, military logistics, and the Arthashastra's detailed camp-planning provisions
Kautilya's preference for maula forces and skepticism of mercenaries — strategic rationale

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Concept of Anvikshaki (Philosophy/Critical Inquiry)
key_dimensions: Anvikshaki as the 'lamp of all sciences' and 'foundation of all actions' — Kautilya's unique elevation of philosophy
Three philosophical schools under Anvikshaki: Sankhya, Yoga, Lokayata — inclusion of materialist Lokayata is significant
Distinction from Tridanda (Triple Vedas) — Anvikshaki as rational-critical thinking separate from scriptural authority
UPSC trap: Kautilya includes Lokayata (Charvaka materialism) as legitimate — suggests pragmatic, non-dogmatic approach to statecraft

concepts.name: Comparison of Arthashastra with Megasthenes' Indica
key_dimensions: Areas of corroboration: royal palace description, seven-caste social division (vs. Arthashastra's varna), municipal administration of Pataliputra
Areas of contradiction: Megasthenes says no slavery; Arthashastra details slave categories — scholarly reconciliation
Megasthenes' six-committee municipal system of Pataliputra vs. Arthashastra's Nagaraka (city superintendent) system
UPSC trap: Indica does NOT survive as original text — known only through fragments in later Greek writers (Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus)

concepts.name: Arthashastra and Machiavelli's Prince — Comparative Political Thought
key_dimensions: Similarities: realpolitik, end-justifies-means in statecraft, separation of morality from political necessity
Key differences: Arthashastra covers economics, law, administration — far broader than The Prince; written ~1800 years earlier
Kautilya's ultimate goal is dharmic state welfare vs. Machiavelli's focus on ruler's personal power retention
UPSC trap: Calling Kautilya 'Indian Machiavelli' is contested — Arthashastra has strong welfare-state and legal dimensions absent in Machiavelli

concepts.name: Arthashastra's Relevance to Mauryan Administrative Reality
key_dimensions: Debate: Is Arthashastra a manual that Chandragupta/Ashoka actually followed, or an ideal-type prescription?
Archaeological corroboration: Ashokan edicts on Rajuka (officials), Dhamma Mahamatra, taxation — partial overlap with Arthashastra
Divergence: Ashoka's Dhamma policy contradicts Arthashastra's purely instrumental statecraft — the 'Ashokan deviation'
UPSC trap: Do NOT treat Arthashastra as a 'factual record' of Mauryan administration — it is prescriptive; corroboration requires cross-referencing
